Question: Describe target architecture for enterprise-scale: active-active or active-passive across regions, RPO/RTO commitments, failover automation, blast radius of single-component failure.
Response: Target architecture: active-passive across Azure paired regions with active-active capability within a region (availability zones). RPO: near-zero for workflow state (Cosmos DB continuous backup with geo-replication). RTO: <5 minutes via automated failover (Azure Traffic Manager for APIM, Cosmos DB automatic failover, Durable Functions checkpoint replay in secondary region). Blast radius containment: (1) Single agentic loop failure — only the current phase is affected. Durable Functions retries from checkpoint. (2) Single Hosted Agent failure — Foundry restarts the container. In-flight sessions are lost but workflow state persists. Next session picks up from last checkpoint. (3) Single MCP tool failure — APIM circuit breaker activates. Workflows depending on that tool enter exception state. Other workflows continue unaffected. (4) Region failure — Traffic Manager routes to paired region. Cosmos DB serves from secondary. Durable Functions replays from geo-replicated checkpoints. Fleet Manager in secondary region takes over. All components are designed for independent failure — no single component failure cascades across the fleet.
Key Technologies: Azure paired regions, Cosmos DB geo-replication, Azure Traffic Manager, Durable Functions checkpoint replay, APIM circuit breakers
POC Demo: POC1: Simulate component failures — show blast radius containment and automatic recovery at each level.

Question: At 40,000 agent-equivalents, what are the bottlenecks (inference, state store, orchestration, tool throughput)? Provide reference architectures at 10x, 50x, 100x current scale with cost modelling.
Response: Scale analysis by component. At 50,000 concurrent workflows: (1) Inference — primary bottleneck. Mitigated by: tiered model usage (only 10-20% of phases need frontier models), semantic caching in APIM, crystallised skills bypassing inference entirely. APIM load balances across multiple model deployments. (2) State store — Cosmos DB scales horizontally with automatic partitioning. 50,000 workflow state documents is well within Cosmos DB's capacity (millions of RU/s). (3) Orchestration — Durable Functions scales with Azure Storage (task hubs partition across storage accounts). 50,000 concurrent orchestrations is supported at Azure's scale. (4) Tool throughput — external system APIs are the actual constraint. APIM rate limiting prevents overwhelming external systems. MCP servers can be scaled independently. Reference architectures at 10x/50x/100x to be provided as a separate deliverable with cost modelling based on WPP's specific workload patterns (phase frequency, model tier distribution, HITL rates).
Key Technologies: Cosmos DB (horizontal scaling), Durable Functions (partitioned task hubs), APIM (load balancing), tiered model deployments

Question: Can the platform deploy across Azure, AWS, and GCP with on-premises components? Describe cross-cloud agent collaboration and consistent behaviour regardless of hosting.
Response: We propose Azure as the primary platform. The architecture is Azure-native: Foundry Hosted Agents, Durable Functions, Cosmos DB, APIM, Entra ID, and Log Analytics are all Azure services. Multi-cloud data access: MCP servers can connect to data sources on any cloud — Databricks on AWS, BigQuery on GCP, on-premises databases. APIM can proxy to APIs hosted anywhere. WPP's existing multi-cloud data layer (Databricks, Snowflake, GCP) is accessible via MCP tools without migrating data to Azure. Cross-cloud agent collaboration: A2A protocol enables agents on different clouds to collaborate. GHCP SDK is open-source and can be run on any cloud — if WPP needs agents on GCP for specific workloads, GHCP SDK agentic loops can run there and communicate with Azure-hosted components via A2A and MCP. However, the governance and orchestration layer (Foundry, APIM, Durable Functions) is Azure-hosted. This is the recommended architecture — centralised governance on Azure with multi-cloud data access.
Key Technologies: Azure (primary), MCP (multi-cloud data access), A2A (cross-cloud agent collaboration), GHCP SDK (portable runtime)

Question: How does the platform avoid single-vendor lock-in: model abstraction, state store abstraction, tool layer abstraction (MCP/A2A)? Describe the exit strategy if we need to migrate off your platform.
Response: Lock-in mitigation at every layer. (1) Model abstraction — GHCP SDK works with any model from the Foundry catalog (1900+ models including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Mistral, and open-source). No proprietary model dependency. Model routing through APIM means switching models is a configuration change. (2) State store — workflow state is JSON in Cosmos DB. Exportable via standard APIs. Durable Functions state is in Azure Storage. Both are extractable. (3) Tool layer — MCP is an open standard. All enterprise integrations are MCP servers. MCP servers are portable to any platform that supports the protocol. (4) Agent logic — GHCP SDK is open-source (MIT licence). Skills are markdown files. WPP retains the ability to self-host, fork, or migrate. (5) A2A — open standard. Agent definitions using A2A are portable. (6) Orchestration — Durable Functions is Azure-specific, but the pattern (event-driven workflow orchestration) is reproducible on any cloud (Temporal, Step Functions). Exit strategy: export skills (Git), export MCP servers (code), export state (Cosmos DB export), export policies (APIM export). The agentic logic is in portable artefacts, not locked to proprietary services.
Key Technologies: GHCP SDK (MIT open-source), MCP (open standard), A2A (open standard), OTEL (open standard), Git (skills), exportable state

Question: Describe cross-region replication of state stores, workflow queues, and memory layers. Demonstrate recovery of an in-flight multi-step workflow after a region failure with no data loss.
Response: Cross-region replication across all stateful components. (1) Workflow state store — Cosmos DB with multi-region writes and continuous backup. Point-in-time restore to any second in the last 30 days. Geo-replication to paired region with automatic failover. (2) Orchestration state — Durable Functions checkpoints stored in Azure Storage with geo-redundant storage (GRS). Secondary region has replicated checkpoints. (3) OTEL telemetry — Application Insights supports cross-region data replication. (4) Audit logs — Azure Log Analytics with geo-redundant archive tier. Recovery of in-flight workflow: (1) Region A fails. (2) Traffic Manager routes to Region B. (3) Cosmos DB serves workflow state from geo-replica — no data loss. (4) Durable Functions in Region B replays from geo-replicated checkpoint — resumes from last completed phase. (5) Fleet Manager in Region B takes over fleet governance. (6) Maximum data loss: the current in-flight agentic loop session (ephemeral, not checkpointed mid-session). The phase replays from the start. No workflow-level data loss.
Key Technologies: Cosmos DB (multi-region, continuous backup), Azure Storage GRS, Azure Traffic Manager, Durable Functions replay
POC Demo: POC1: Simulate region failure mid-workflow — show recovery in secondary region with workflow resuming from last checkpoint. Demonstrate no data loss on workflow state.

Question: Describe unified observability across the agent fleet: OpenTelemetry support, custom dashboards, anomaly detection, cost attribution per agent type, client, and market at millions of traces per day.
Response: Unified observability through OTEL standards across the entire fleet. (1) OpenTelemetry — every agentic loop emits OTEL spans via TracerProvider. Spans carry: workflow ID, phase, jurisdiction, model, token count, cost, duration. Foundry Tracing provides native OTEL integration with full trace visualisation. (2) Custom dashboards — Foundry Control Plane for platform monitoring. Custom Control Plane UI for operator experience. Application Insights workbooks for technical investigation. Power BI for executive reporting. All consuming the same telemetry data. (3) Anomaly detection — APIM statistical baselines, Foundry Evaluator drift detection, Fleet Manager fleet-wide pattern analysis. Alerts via Azure Monitor. (4) Cost attribution — per workflow, per phase, per model, per tool, per agent type, per client, per market. Sourced from APIM token metrics and OTEL cost spans. Aggregable at any dimension. (5) Scale — Application Insights supports ingestion of millions of traces per day. Log Analytics handles petabyte-scale data with performant queries via KQL. APIM metrics scale with Azure Monitor infrastructure. At 50,000 concurrent workflows with ~10 phases each, this is ~500,000 active traces — well within Application Insights capacity.
Key Technologies: Foundry Tracing (OTEL), Application Insights, APIM metrics, Fleet Manager, Azure Monitor, Custom Control Plane UI, Power BI
POC Demo: POC1: Show unified observability — OTEL traces for invoice workflows with cost attribution. Custom dashboards at fleet scale. Anomaly detection alert.
